pr_title: ARM: Make FPU Sharing the default mode and activate Lazy FP stacking dynamically
pr_body:
Fixes #29590 ( Also fixes #31472, which was reporting an in-tree failure, related to the same thing)
Fixes #28014

The PR does the following

1. Force FP sharing mode when we build with FPU support, effectively making the FP Sharing the default Floating Point services mode in Cortex-M
2. When MPU Stack Guard feature is enabled, activate the Lazy FP stacking functionality dynamically, for the threads actively using the FP registers
    - some extra logic is implemented on the context-switch (only under #ifdef MPU_STACK_GUARD, which is a debug feature)
    - saves threads from the need for large MPU guards if they are not using the FP registers, while still guaranteeing stack overflow detection

issue_context.title: tests: kernel: poll: timeout with FPU enabled
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**
When running tests/kernel/poll on stm32f3_disco, test never ends and twister timeout expires.
This happens specially on stm32f3_disco which has CONFIG_FPU enabled by default.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. twister -N --device-testing --hardware-map ../map.yaml -c -p stm32f3_disco -T tests/kernel/poll/
2. Test never ends and twister timeout expires

**Expected behavior**
Tests passed

**Logs and console output**
*** Booting Zephyr OS build zephyr-v2.4.0-3063-g33028963c808  ***
```
Running test suite poll_api
===================================================================
START - test_poll_no_wait
E: syscall z_vrfy_k_poll failed check: num_events too large
E: syscall z_vrfy_k_poll failed check: e->mode == K_POLL_MODE_NOTIFY_ONLY
PASS - test_poll_no_wait
===================================================================
START - test_poll_wait
PASS - test_poll_wait
===================================================================
START - test_poll_zero_events
PASS - test_poll_zero_events
===================================================================
START - test_poll_cancel_main_low_prio
PASS - test_poll_cancel_main_low_prio
===================================================================
START - test_poll_cancel_main_high_prio
PASS - test_poll_cancel_main_high_prio
===================================================================
START - test_poll_multi
PASS - test_poll_multi
===================================================================
START - test_poll_threadstate
```


**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - OS:  Linux
 - Toolchain: Zephyr SDK
 - Commit SHA 33028963c808428e2c6dadad6bff556ddec3f67a
comments:
**Reproducibility:**
Issue is not reproducible on windows (probably due to different toolchain).
It is only reproducible when compiler size optimization is enabled (CONFIG_SIZE_OPTIMIZATIONS)
Issue is specially reproducible on stm32f3_disco because, with stm32373c_eval, they are the only stm32 boards for which FPU is enabled by default.

**Analysis:**
During the test, there is thread creation in test framework run_test().
Despite C code explicitly requesting creation with K_NO_WAIT as 'delay' parameter (i.e. 0x0),
this parameter, at some point, somehow, get 0xFFFFFFFF value and this explains that test never ends and that twister timeout expires.

Analyzing deeper, and looking at assembly code,
I found that K_NO_WAIT value is stored in d8 FPU register at the beginning of z_ztest_run_test_suite()
and thanks to optimization, it is supposed to remain in d8 for all further subtest (for each call to run_test())
But in fact, when reaching 'test_poll_threadstate' subtest, it appears that d8 has been modifie, resulting in delay=0xFFFFFFFF.

Debugging step by step I could not found which code modified d8,
I guess that it occurs during interrupts, or zephyr thread switch.
And I wonder whether zephyr guarantee preservation of FPU registers (with Lazy stacking for interrupt and during thread switch).
CONFIG_FPU_SHARING seems to do that  (enabling FPU Lazy stacking for interrupt)
but this switch  is not enabled for stm32f3_disco.
When I enabled CONFIG_FPU_SHARING , test is passed (in condition to increase CONFIG_MAIN_STACK_SIZE).

**Questions:**
As compiler is able, in any thread, to use FPU registers like general purpose registers (even when no floating point computation is performed),
should FPU_SHARING be enabled automatically (KConfig) when FPU is enabled ? (and maybe under other conditions like multithreadding ... ?)

Note: enabling FPU_SHARING requires to increase some (all ?) stacks in order to avoid stack overflow.
So in such case should we also increase stacks (MAIN_STACK_SIZE, ZTEST_STACKSIZE,...) automatically (KConfig) when CONFIG_FPU_SHARING is enabled ?

Enabling CONFIG_FPU_SHARING (and increasing CONFIG_MAIN_STACK_SIZE),
also solves other issues on stm32f3_disco:
* tests/kernel/semaphore/semaphore
* tests/kernel/pipe/pipe_api
* tests/kernel/sched/preempt
* tests/benchmarks/app_kernel/
This might be related to #29590 (based on CONFIG_FPU_SHARING need).

@ABOSTM thanks for the detailed analysis, I am going to take a look.

Enabling FPU_SHARING would be a straightforward fix that comes with a cost of extra ram, code footprint and context-switch overhead, so I'd rather avoid this if possible.
Closing this ticket as it concerns the same issue as #29590

review_comments: Should we add test configuration to force  CONFIG_MPU_STACK_GUARD activation and be sure it is tested ?
Oh, but this should be done by default, @ABOSTM, I guess, by default, ztests are enabling HW_STACK_PROTECTION, which gives MPU_STACK_GUARD on ARMv7-M.

I think we should handle both LSPEN (Lazy stacking) and ASPEN (automatic state preservation) at the same time:
https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dai0298/a/
My understanding is that in our case we should switch between
* (LSPEN=0, ASPEN=0) no FPU context preservation 
* (LSPEN=1, ASPEN=1)  FPU preservation with Lazy stacking

(LSPEN=0, ASPEN=1)  automatic FPU preservation without lazy stacking will stack register unconditionally,
whereas (LSPEN=1, ASPEN=1)  will reserve registers in stack but effective stacking occurs only if ISR make use of FPU registers.
So (1, 1) is more performant, (and thus (0, 1) is useless in our case)

Well, ASPEN=1 is mandatory for FPU_SHARING case, we cannot get around without it. The reason is that ASPEN=1 is needed to set CONTROL.FPCA as soon as the thread activates FP context; otherwise there's no way you can tell that a thread _is_ actually using the FP registers (and do the save/restore of callee-saved s16-s31 at swap)

Here's how i see it, let me know if you have concerns:

1. ASPEN=1 always, when FPU_SHARING=y.
2. LSPEN=1, always, when we _don't_ use MPU guards
3. When we use MPU guards, switch between:
    - (LSPEN=0, ASPEN=1) FPU context preservation without lazy stacking
        - for the threads that are not have an active FP context currently, so they won't really need to stack anything. I need to disable Lazy Stacking here, to be able to use a small MPU guard (32 instead of 128). If these threads start using FPU, then, until the first swap, there's no Lazy Stacking, so there's some temporary ISR penalty. But then the will switch to the case below:
    - (LSPEN=1, ASPEN=1) FPU preservation with Lazy stacking
        - for the threads that have been using FPU so it is important to keep ISR latency low, to the cost of having to use more stack memory for the guard.

The optimization, here, is that if a thread is _unlikely_ to use FPU, better to be saving the RAM, and de-activate LSPEN. LSPEN is not needed if there are no FPU instructions at the thread, but memory is needed. Then, as soon as a thread becomes FPU-user, the focus is on ISR performance, instead of memory.
Again, this only applies when we do MPU_STACK_GUARD, which is a rather debug feature.

My understanding is that:
* (LSPEN=1, ASPEN=1): FPU registers stacking is unconditional at ISR entry
* (LSPEN=0, ASPEN=1): Space for FPU registers are reserved in stack at ISR entry, and effective stacking occurs only if ISR make use of FPU registers.

So deactivating Lazy stacking will not save memory in stack, as in both cases, space is reserved in stack.
The only effect if CPU efficiency when Lazy stacking is enabled (we can avoid register copy when ISR don't use FPU)

So as long as ASPEN=1, I think we should keep also LSPEN=1.

@ABOSTM Your understanding is correct, however:

> So deactivating Lazy stacking will not save memory in stack, as in both cases, space is reserved in stack.
The only effect if CPU efficiency when Lazy stacking is enabled (we can avoid register copy when ISR don't use FPU)

Assume a thread that executes code that is not using the FPU. Even with ASPEN=1, this thread won't stack any FP context. Assume, also that I would like to use MPU guard to catch stack overflow. If I use a 32 byte MPU guard, at most of the times I will be able to catch occurring stack overflows. However, if, at some point the thread starts using the FPU and a stack overflow occurs, there is a problem: if LSTEN=1, the exception will reserve the memory for the FPU stacking, move the stack pointer 96 bytes below, and _there_ it will stack the standard ESF. So the 32 byte long MPU guard won't help us catch the overflow (very bad thing). I have two solutions
1. Keep LSTEN=1 and use _always an 128 byte-long MPU guard; this one is big enough to accommodate both the FP context ("empty" when LSTEN=1) and the default ESF context. But this is a waste of memory, because this 128 guard cannot be used by the thread. If threads are really not-likely to use FPU, this seems like a waste.
2. Keep MPU size at 32 bytes and set LSTEN=0 for threads that do not use the FPU. For such threads it clearly plays no role whether LSTEN or ASTEN is 0 or 1. **In the case that these threads will start using the FPU** then, since lazy stacking is disabled, the 32 byte guard is good enough to catch any stack overflow (cause the FP regs will be really written to the stack), so our HW stack protection works as specified. In the mean time, I am able to give back to the thread 128 - 32 = 96 bytes for stack usage. There is only one **temporary penalty**; increased ISR latency for the IRQs occurring from the point the thread started using the FPU, until it is swapped out. That's because **the next time the thread swaps in**, the thread configuration will switch to solution [1].

Say, you have an application with N threads, but only a couple of them will use the FPU, then, with option [2] you can save 96 * (N-2) bytes from wasting, while you are still comfortable that your Stack Overflow detection is fully working.

Once more, that's only when MPU Guards are enabled (other wise ASPEN=1, LSPEN=1 is the fixed configuration).

Ok I got your point, and understand the MPU guards implication.
Thanks for the clarifications.
